interactions: Methotrexate: no pharmacokinetic interaction expected; both drugs can raise transaminases, so coordinate liver test monitoring with rheumatology and review the methotrexate dose if ALT rises.
Hydroxychloroquine: no clinically significant interaction expected.

Alendronate: no interaction with riluzole; oral bisphosphonates need an upright posture and can injure the oesophagus, so review it with the prescriber because swallowing is already affected.
output.summary: No interaction requires a change to riluzole 50 mg twice daily; methotrexate can also raise transaminases, so coordinate liver test monitoring with rheumatology and review the methotrexate dose if ALT rises. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for the first 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x ULN. Report any febrile illness (check the white cell count for neutropenia).
warnings: Hepatotoxicity: measure ALT and AST before the first dose, monthly for the first 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x ULN.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Fibrillation potentials with chronic neurogenic change and complex fasciculations in cervical myotomes; fibrillations in the tongue, mentalis and T6-T8 paraspinals; fasciculations, mildly large MUPs and sparse fibrillations in tibialis anterior; reduced median and ulnar CMAPs with normal conduction velocities and no conduction block; normal sensory studies.
action_criteria.label: EMG and nerve conduction studies of the bulbar, cervical, thoracic and lumbosacral regions to document lower motor neuron involvement and exclude conduction block and neuropathy
action_criteria.rationale: EMG/NCS confirms lower motor neuron involvement beyond the clinically affected muscles and excludes the main treatable mimics: multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block, demyelinating or sensorimotor neuropathy and myopathy. Gold Coast 2020 accepts EMG evidence of lower motor neuron dysfunction, and Awaji 2008 counts fasciculation potentials as active denervation in muscles with chronic neurogenic change.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No infarct, hemorrhage, mass or demyelinating lesion; subtle nonspecific corticospinal tract signal change is supportive only.
action_criteria.label: Brain MRI to exclude structural, vascular, demyelinating, inflammatory or neoplastic causes of the upper motor neuron or bulbar signs
action_criteria.rationale: MRI does not confirm ALS. It excludes brain and brainstem lesions that can cause upper motor neuron or bulbar signs; corticospinal tract signal change, when present, is supportive only.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Mild C3-C6 degenerative change with mild foraminal narrowing and no cord compression or signal change; no rheumatoid pannus at C1-C2; normal thoracic cord.
action_criteria.label: Spine MRI of the cervical and thoracic cord, and of the lumbosacral spine when lower limb signs need it, to exclude compressive myelopathy, radiculopathy and other cord lesions
action_criteria.rationale: Cervical spondylotic myelopathy with radiculopathy is the commonest structural mimic of combined upper and lower motor neuron signs in the limbs. Spine MRI excludes it, but incidental spondylosis does not explain bulbar signs or denervation in other regions and must not delay the ALS work-up.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: CK 580 U/L (3.4x ULN), ESR 58 mm/hr, CRP 12.4 mg/L and hemoglobin 11.8 g/dL; renal and liver function, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate normal.
action_criteria.label: Blood tests for treatable mimics and a pre-treatment baseline: full blood count, renal and liver function, electrolytes and calcium, CK, thyroid function, vitamin B12 and folate, ESR and CRP
action_criteria.rationale: These tests exclude metabolic, endocrine, nutritional and inflammatory mimics and give the liver and blood-count baseline needed before riluzole; phenotype-specific tests are added only when the case raises that mimic.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Reduced FVC (76% predicted) and SNIP (55 cmH2O): inspiratory muscle weakness already present at baseline.
action_criteria.label: Baseline respiratory function (FVC and SNIP, with MIP where available) to stage respiratory muscle involvement and plan monitoring and NIV
action_criteria.rationale: Respiratory function does not diagnose ALS. Once ALS is supported it stages respiratory muscle weakness, sets the baseline for 3-monthly monitoring and identifies patients who need early referral for NIV.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: No pathogenic variant on the ALS gene panel; a negative result does not exclude a genetic contribution.
action_criteria.label: ALS gene panel (C9orf72 repeat expansion; SOD1, TARDBP, FUS and TBK1) after pre-test genetic counselling, once the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment is complete
action_criteria.rationale: Genetic testing does not make the diagnosis. It is offered with counselling to people with ALS because a pathogenic variant changes counselling for relatives and may open gene-targeted treatment or trials.

action_criteria.expected_evidence: Methotrexate and riluzole can both raise transaminases: liver monitoring coordinated with rheumatology and a methotrexate dose review if ALT rises; no interaction with hydroxychloroquine, folic acid or losartan; oral alendronate reviewed because swallowing is affected; riluzole stopped if ALT exceeds 5x ULN.
action_criteria.label: Check riluzole against the current medicines, alcohol use and liver function before the first dose, once the diagnosis is established
action_criteria.rationale: Riluzole is metabolised by CYP1A2 and can raise liver transaminases, so the medicine list, alcohol use and baseline liver function are reviewed before treatment. Methotrexate can also raise transaminases, so liver monitoring is coordinated with rheumatology and the methotrexate dose reviewed if ALT rises.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not treat ALS with corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange: they have no benefit.
Do not wait for FVC to fall below 50% or for respiratory symptoms before referring for NIV assessment.
Do not delay the swallowing assessment in a patient who already has difficulty swallowing solid food.
Do not refer for cervical spine surgery on the basis of the mild C3-C6 spondylotic changes: they do not explain the bulbar signs or the denervation in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles.
required_recommendations: Make and explain the diagnosis of ALS by Gold Coast 2020 criteria: progressive bilateral arm weakness with hand wasting, now with bulbar symptoms, with upper motor neuron signs (brisk arm and knee reflexes, bilateral Hoffman signs and a left extensor plantar response) and lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions on examination and EMG, with active denervation also in bulbar (tongue, mentalis) and thoracic paraspinal muscles, with mimics excluded by MRI and blood tests; disclose it in a planned face-to-face discussion with the patient and family.

Refer to the respiratory/NIV service now because FVC (76% predicted) and SNIP (55 cmH2O) are already reduced; screen for orthopnoea and nocturnal hypoventilation with overnight oximetry or capnography, and repeat FVC and SNIP within 3 months.

Arrange a speech and language therapy swallowing assessment now (aspiration risk, safe food and fluid consistencies) and a dietetic review with baseline weight, and discuss gastrostomy early, while FVC is above 50% predicted.

Offer riluzole 50 mg twice daily. Measure liver transaminases before the first dose, monthly for 3 months, every 3 months for the rest of the first year and periodically thereafter; stop riluzole if ALT exceeds 5x the upper limit of normal, and ask the patient to report any febrile illness so that neutropenia can be excluded.
Coordinate liver-function monitoring with rheumatology because methotrexate and riluzole can both raise transaminases, and review oral alendronate given dysphagia.

Refer to a specialist ALS multidisciplinary team (neurologist, specialist nurse, respiratory, speech and language therapy, dietetics, physiotherapy, occupational therapy and palliative care), reviewed about every 2 to 3 months, with an early, patient-paced discussion of advance care planning.
Offer genetic counselling and, if the patient wishes, ALS genetic testing, explaining the implications for relatives.

avoided_actions.rationale: ALS is a motor-neuron disease without cortical electrical signature; EEG has no diagnostic role and adds cost without benefit.
ECG is unrelated to motor neuron disease and not part of the standard ALS workup absent specific cardiac symptoms or pre-medication QTc checks.
Echocardiography is unrelated to ALS diagnosis; no indication absent comorbid cardiac disease.
Cardiac monitoring has no role in ALS diagnostic workup.
MRI is the standard structural study for ALS workup; head CT adds no diagnostic value and exposes the patient to ionizing radiation.
Amyloid PET has no role in ALS diagnosis (motor-neuron rather than amyloid pathology) and carries a high cost.
DaTscan evaluates nigrostriatal dopaminergic integrity; it has no role in ALS, which spares the dopaminergic system.
FDG-PET has no established diagnostic role in ALS and adds substantial cost.

accepted: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) with concurrent rheumatoid arthritis

differential.diagnosis: Rheumatoid arthritis-related muscle or tendon disease (including inflammatory myositis)
differential.key_features: supports: active seropositive RA with MCP and PIP deformities, ESR 58 mm/hr, CRP 12.4 mg/L and CK 580 U/L; against: thenar and intrinsic hand wasting with fasciculations, tongue fasciculations, upper motor neuron signs, and a neurogenic rather than myopathic EMG.

supports: active RA with raised inflammatory markers; against: no new sensory symptoms and no sensory signs, normal sensory conduction, symmetric denervation in four regions and upper motor neuron signs.
supports: age 71, hand weakness and raised CK; against: neurogenic EMG, thenar and intrinsic rather than finger flexor and quadriceps weakness, fasciculations and upper motor neuron signs.

differential.diagnosis: Cervical myelopathy from rheumatoid cervical spine disease
differential.key_features: supports: long-standing RA with arm weakness, hyperreflexia and Hoffman signs; against: no pannus, cord compression or cord signal change on spine MRI, and bulbar, thoracic and lumbosacral denervation.

supports: long-term hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily with raised CK and proximal arm weakness; against: no myopathic motor units, prominent fasciculations, tongue denervation and upper motor neuron signs.
supports: weekly methotrexate with raised CK; against: methotrexate rarely causes myopathy, and the EMG is neurogenic with fasciculations and upper motor neuron signs.

key_clinical_evidence: Gold Coast 2020: ALS needs progressive motor impairment with upper and lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least one body region, or lower motor neuron dysfunction in at least two, after other diseases are excluded. Here: brisk arm and knee reflexes, bilateral Hoffman signs and a left extensor plantar response with lower motor neuron involvement in the cervical and lumbosacral regions, with active denervation also in bulbar (tongue, mentalis) and thoracic paraspinal muscles (upper-limb-onset ALS phenotype).
EMG lower motor neuron evidence is chronic neurogenic change with active denervation; by Awaji 2008 fasciculation potentials count as active denervation in a muscle with chronic neurogenic change.

Normal motor conduction velocities without conduction block argue against multifocal motor neuropathy, and normal sensory responses argue against a sensorimotor neuropathy, including RA-associated vasculitic neuropathy.
CK 580 U/L (3.4x ULN): mild to moderate elevation is common in ALS from denervation and does not by itself suggest a myopathy.

FVC 76% predicted and SNIP 55 cmH2O are reduced, indicating early inspiratory muscle weakness. AAN 2009 markers that prompt NIV discussion are orthopnoea, FVC below 50% predicted, SNIP below 40 cmH2O, MIP weaker than -60 cmH2O or abnormal overnight oximetry; NIV prolongs survival and improves quality of life (Bourke 2006).

Mild C3-C6 spondylotic changes are common at this age, and the MRI shows no rheumatoid pannus or cord compression; neither could explain the bulbar signs or the denervation in thoracic and lumbosacral muscles.
Bulbar involvement carries a worse prognosis and an aspiration risk; swallowing assessment and early gastrostomy discussion, while FVC is above 50% predicted, are priorities.

red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The raised ESR and CRP and the MCP and PIP deformities reflect RA activity, but RA does not explain tongue fasciculations, upper motor neuron signs, preserved sensation and motor denervation in four regions with normal sensory studies; RA is a confounder, not the explanation.
red_herrings.data_point: Active rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate, with raised ESR and CRP and joint deformities
red_herrings.intended_effect: Anchors the weakness and wasting on RA joint, tendon, vasculitic or myopathic disease

sequence_constraints.reason: Genetic testing follows the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment and pre-test counselling; it does not make the diagnosis.
Riluzole is considered only after the clinical and electrodiagnostic assessment supports ALS.

findings.finding: Bilateral first dorsal interosseous, abductor pollicis brevis and extensor digitorum communis: fibrillations +2, positive sharp waves +2, complex fasciculation potentials. Large-amplitude (6-8 mV), long-duration, polyphasic MUPs with severely reduced recruitment. Cervical paraspinals: fibrillations +1 bilaterally.
Tongue: fibrillations +1, fasciculation potentials. Mentalis: fibrillations +1.
Bilateral tibialis anterior: fasciculation potentials, mildly large MUPs, sparse fibrillation potentials.

Median motor: CMAP 2.1 mV right and 3.0 mV left (reduced), distal latencies 4.0 and 3.9 ms, conduction velocities 51 and 52 m/s. Ulnar motor: CMAP 3.4 mV right and 4.1 mV left (reduced), conduction velocities 53 and 54 m/s across the forearm and elbow. Peroneal motor: CMAP 4.2 mV, conduction velocity 44 m/s. Tibial motor: CMAP 7.8 mV, conduction velocity 43 m/s. No conduction block, temporal dispersion or multifocal slowing.
Median, ulnar, radial and sural sensory studies: normal amplitudes and conduction velocities.

specialized_test.impression: 1. Active denervation (fibrillation potentials, positive sharp waves) with chronic neurogenic change (large, long-duration, polyphasic MUPs with severely reduced recruitment) and complex fasciculation potentials in cervical myotomes bilaterally, with cervical paraspinal fibrillations. 2. Fibrillation and fasciculation potentials in the tongue and fibrillation potentials in mentalis. 3. Fibrillation potentials in the T6-T8 paraspinals. 4. Fasciculation potentials, mildly large MUPs and sparse fibrillation potentials in tibialis anterior bilaterally. 5. Reduced median and ulnar CMAP amplitudes with normal distal latencies and conduction velocities; no conduction block. Sensory studies normal. The findings indicate a widespread disorder of anterior horn cells.

patient.history_present_illness:
Mrs. B is a 71-year-old left-handed woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis who presents with an 11-month history of progressive bilateral arm weakness and hand wasting. She and her rheumatologist initially attributed her progressive hand weakness to worsening RA-related joint disease, tendon involvement, or possible vasculitis.

Over the past 6 months, she noticed prominent wasting of the muscles between her fingers and at the base of her thumbs bilaterally, out of proportion to her joint swelling. She has also seen twitching in both arms at rest.

She has had progressive difficulty lifting objects, reaching overhead, and using scissors. Over the past 3-4 months she has noticed mild swallowing difficulties with solid foods. Her husband noted her speech occasionally sounds different. She denies new sensory symptoms; occasional hand numbness that she has had with RA flares is unchanged.

Her rheumatologist considered RA-related causes, including vasculitic mononeuritis multiplex and an inflammatory myopathy, and referred her to neurology for evaluation of the weakness, wasting and twitching.
